# Face Culling and Visibility Optimization

Also called: Interior Polygon Removal, Removing Interior Polygons

## Overview
Face Culling and Visibility Optimization reduces the rendering load in [blocky meshing](#31-blocky-meshing.md) by reconstructing cubes from triangles and removing sides that are adjacent to solid neighbors, thereby avoiding the rendering of hidden geometry [S1, unofficial]. It solves the problem of naively rendering all 6 faces of every cube, including those hidden by neighbors, which results in excessive geometry and poor performance [S1, unofficial]. It sets itself apart from its siblings by operating at the fundamental voxel adjacency level during mesh creation, rather than relying on post-generation mesh filtering, coverage masks, or runtime visibility checks [S1, unofficial].

## Shared principles
The core mechanism involves iterating through occupied voxel positions and checking for neighbors in the 6 cardinal directions (Up, Down, Left, Right, Front, Back). If a neighbor exists, the face between the current voxel and the neighbor is occluded and skipped; if no neighbor exists, the face is exposed and added to the mesh [S1, unofficial].

The visibility condition for a face between voxel $A$ and neighbor $B$ is defined as:
$$ \text{Visible} = \neg \text{Occluded}(A, B) $$
Where $\text{Occluded}(A, B)$ is true if neighbor $B$ is solid [Parent].

For bitmask-based implementations, visibility is calculated using bitwise operations on a mask $M$ where bit $i$ is 1 if voxel $i$ is solid and 0 if it is air [S2, unofficial]. For a 1D slice, the visible left faces are:
$$ F_{left} = M \ \& \ \sim(M >> 1) $$
And the visible right faces are:
$$ F_{right} = M \ \& \ \sim(M << 1) $$
Where $\sim$ is bitwise NOT, $>>$ is bitwise right shift, and $<<$ is bitwise left shift [S2, unofficial].

## Subtopics

### [Voxel Block Shape & Culling Configuration](2176-voxel-block-shape-culling-configuration.md)
This method defines a trait-based configuration system that maps individual voxel block types to specific geometric shapes, transparency culling modes, and lighting values. It solves the problem of hard-coded mesh generation logic by allowing different block types (e.g., glass, fluids, slopes) to dictate their own rendering behavior, thereby supporting complex geometries and varied [transparency handling](#3611-order-independent-transparency-approaches.md) without modifying the core meshing algorithm. It sets itself apart from generic [face culling](#8735-face-culling.md) by binding culling rules directly to the block's semantic identity rather than just its occupancy status.

### [Face Coverage Mask Culling](3397-face-coverage-mask-culling.md)
[Face Coverage Mask Culling](#3397-face-coverage-mask-culling.md) is a method for removing hidden faces of partial voxel shapes (such as stairs, slabs, or custom geometries) by representing face coverage as a bit mask. It solves the problem where a boolean "solid/empty" flag is insufficient because partial shapes have mixed visible and hidden areas on a single face. Unlike sibling methods that rely on coarse block visibility or vertex packing, this method operates at the sub-face granularity, allowing precise culling of geometry that is occluded by neighbors while preserving exposed portions of the same face.

### [ChunkMesh Vertex Packing and Management](3566-chunkmesh-vertex-packing-and-management.md)
[ChunkMesh Vertex Packing and Management](#3566-chunkmesh-vertex-packing-and-management.md) is a dynamic mesh generation and memory management technique for voxel terrain that packs vertex attributes into compact 32-bit integers and manages buffer updates via a free-list allocator. It solves the problem of high memory overhead and frequent GPU buffer uploads in blocky meshing by reducing vertex data size and enabling efficient incremental updates. It differs from static meshing by supporting runtime addition/removal of blocks with neighbor synchronization, and from pure culling methods by actively managing the vertex buffer layout and reuse.

### [Voxel Backface Culling and Internal Face Masking](4569-voxel-backface-culling-and-internal-face-masking.md)
This method optimizes voxel mesh rendering by rejecting faces that are either occluded by adjacent voxels (internal faces) or oriented away from the camera (backfaces). It distinguishes itself from standard neighbor-check culling by performing visibility tests in projection space to determine front/back orientation, while using a compact bitmask to track internal occlusion, allowing for efficient geometry shader-based culling.

### [Block Visibility Culling](5334-block-visibility-culling.md)
[Block Visibility Culling](#5334-block-visibility-culling.md) determines which voxel blocks require mesh updates or rendering by evaluating the camera's position and rotation relative to block coordinates, avoiding unnecessary geometry generation when the viewing direction or position has not changed significantly. It operates at the coarse block level, using camera-relative orientation to cull entire blocks or specific faces based on whether they are visible to the viewer, distinct from fine-grained face-level checks.

### [Extraction of Surface Points (Sobierajski)](5721-extraction-of-surface-points-sobierajski.md)
A fast display method for direct rendering of boundary surfaces by extracting only visible boundary voxels from volume data. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like [Voxel Block Shape & Culling Configuration](2176-voxel-block-shape-culling-configuration.md) by operating on individual voxels rather than blocks, and from [Face Culling and Visibility Optimization](3861-face-culling-and-visibility-optimization.md) by explicitly using multi-view orthographic projection to determine visibility before generating geometry, thereby reducing the voxel list size prior to rendering.

### [Mask Projection Culling](6836-mask-projection-culling.md)
[Mask Projection Culling](#6836-mask-projection-culling.md) is a visibility-based mesh filtering technique that removes faces and vertices not consistently observed across multiple camera poses by projecting points into camera space and comparing their depth against rendered depth maps or binary masks. It differs from simple adjacency culling by using actual camera views to determine visibility, allowing it to cull geometry that is occluded by other objects in the scene rather than just adjacent voxels. It differs from [Face Coverage Mask Culling](3397-face-coverage-mask-culling.md) by operating on the final mesh geometry (vertices/faces) rather than pre-computing coverage masks during voxel traversal.

### [Mesh Culling via 3D Projection and Connected Components](6963-mesh-culling-via-3d-projection-and-connected-components.md)
This method reduces mesh noise and artifacts in unbounded reconstructions (such as [Gaussian Splatting](#946-gaussian-splatting.md)) by projecting mesh vertices into multiple camera views and discarding geometry that is not consistently visible across a threshold number of views. It differs from standard adjacency or backface culling by using multi-view consistency to remove floating artifacts and distant noise that do not contribute to the final rendered image from any significant viewpoint. It builds on [Face Culling and Visibility Optimization](3861-face-culling-and-visibility-optimization.md) by applying a global visibility test rather than local voxel adjacency.

### [Face Culling](8735-face-culling.md)
Face Culling is a mesh generation optimization that reduces the number of vertices and triangles sent to the graphics pipeline by skipping the rendering of voxel faces that are adjacent to existing neighboring voxels. It solves the problem of naively rendering all 6 faces of every cube, including those hidden by neighbors, which results in excessive geometry and poor performance. It sets itself apart from its siblings by operating at the fundamental voxel adjacency level during mesh creation, rather than relying on post-generation mesh filtering, coverage masks, or runtime visibility checks.

### [Opacity-based Mesh Culling](8759-opacity-based-mesh-culling.md)
[Opacity-based Mesh Culling](#8759-opacity-based-mesh-culling.md) reduces the triangle count of a generated polygonal mesh by discarding faces that contribute negligible visual information based on their opacity values. It solves the problem of excessive geometry in [neural radiance field (NeRF)](#834-neural-radiance-field-nerf.md) extractions, where many triangles represent transparent or low-density regions. It differs from sibling methods like [Face Culling](8735-face-culling.md) (which relies on geometric adjacency or backface normals) and [Block Visibility Culling](5334-block-visibility-culling.md) (which operates at the voxel block level) by evaluating the material property (opacity) of the mesh faces themselves, often during or after the training phase of a neural representation.

### [From-Region Visibility Preprocessing](9048-from-region-visibility-preprocessing.md)
[From-region visibility preprocessing](#9048-from-region-visibility-preprocessing.md) is a technique that precomputes which geometric primitives are visible from a specific region of the viewing volume, allowing the renderer to discard occluded geometry before the graphics pipeline. It differs from standard backface or adjacency culling by accounting for complex occlusion relationships across the entire scene structure, often involving occluder fusion to reduce the number of visibility tests. While it enables significant runtime performance gains by reducing triangle counts, it is characterized by substantial preprocessing overhead.

### Buried Bitmask Optimization
A bitmask used to track which blocks in a chunk are 'buried' (fully surrounded by opaque blocks), allowing the renderer to skip mesh generation for those blocks [S2, unofficial]. The algorithm resets the buried bitmask for the chunk, creates `MappedAdjacentChunks` for the current chunk position to access neighboring chunks, and iterates through all blocks in the chunk (0 to `CHUNK_SIZE`). For each block, it determines if it is buried by calling `block->isBuried(...)` and sets the corresponding flag in the bitmask [S2, unofficial]. If all blocks in the chunk are buried (checked via `buriedBitmask->AreAllBlocksSet()`), the mesh is marked as empty and mesh generation is skipped [S2, unofficial]. When generating the mesh, any block that is air or has its buried flag set in the bitmask is skipped [S2, unofficial].

### Two-pass transparent meshing with opaque separation
A meshing strategy that separates opaque and transparent geometry into two passes to ensure correct rendering order and reduce overdraw, by generating opaque faces between air/transparent blocks and transparent faces only for blocks touching air [S3, unofficial]. The method first checks if the chunk contains any transparent blocks; if not, the second pass is skipped [S3, unofficial]. In the first (opaque) pass, if the chunk contains transparent blocks, it tests for opaque blocks (ignoring transparent and air) to generate opaque faces between air and transparent blocks; otherwise, it tests for non-air blocks [S3, unofficial]. In the second (transparent) pass, it tests for non-air blocks to mark only transparent blocks, generating faces for all transparent blocks touching air but not adding faces between transparent and solid blocks [S3, unofficial]. Solid block types are filtered out during the transparent pass by checking if the block type is transparent before constructing the AO value and adding the block type to the hashmap [S3, unofficial].

### Smart Leaf Rendering
A leaf block rendering strategy that preserves alpha cutouts on outer leaf surfaces while culling internal faces to reduce vertex count [S4, unofficial]. The behavior is controlled by a global static enum `sLeafRenderMode`, which defaults to `ChunkRenderer::LeafRenderMode::Smart` [S4, unofficial].

## Background
The concept of removing interior polygons to improve rendering performance was documented in the context of voxel-based procedural terrain generation, specifically referencing Minecraft-like engines [S1, unofficial]. The optimization addresses the inefficiency of instantiating models of cubes where only some sides are visible [S1, unofficial]. A class that creates cubes from triangles was added to tools to allow each cube to check for solid neighbors and determine which sides to render [S1, unofficial]. To further optimize, the meshes of all cubes were combined into a single big mesh called a 'chunk' [S1, unofficial]. This introduced constraints such as Unity's limit of ~65,000 vertices per mesh, requiring chunks to be stacked or split [S1, unofficial].
